title: Only now
hook: each lives only this moment; the rest is gone or unknown (Meditations 3.10)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Marcus on revering judgment. Your line was judge carefully. When a verdict popped up, did you catch the gap between what you saw and what you decided? Day five hundred forty-five.

Where are you right now? Not where your body is. Where your mind is. Maybe it's replaying a conversation from Tuesday, or rehearsing one for Friday. The past rides along like a backpack, the future hangs ahead like a weather forecast, and the one place we actually stand gets barely a glance. Marcus Aurelius set all of that down in a few short lines, in the tenth entry of his third book. Today: only now.
screen: `WHERE IS YOUR MIND?` → `TUESDAY BEHIND, FRIDAY AHEAD.` → `ONLY NOW.`

segments.voice: First, throw the rest away. Marcus opens the tenth entry of book three by telling himself to let everything else go and hold on to these few things. It's a clearing-out. Second, the moment. Each of us, he says, lives only the present, this moment that can't be divided. Everything else is either already lived or uncertain. That's not a mood. It's a description. You cannot live yesterday again, and you cannot yet live tomorrow. In his terms, the only life anyone actually has is happening in this breath. Third, how small it all is. Then Marcus widens the lens. Short is the life each person lives. Small is the corner of the earth where they live it. Short, too, is the longest fame after death, and it's passed along by people who will die soon themselves, who don't know even themselves, let alone someone long gone. He's not trying to depress himself. He's pulling his attention back from the places it wanders, the regrets and the legacy, to the one place it can do any good. Fourth, why this is freedom. If the past is finished and the future unknown, then neither one is where your choices happen. The present is small, but it's the only part of life you can steer. Other contemplative traditions have their own words for returning to this moment. For Marcus, it's plain arithmetic. As he put it back in book two, the present is the only thing anyone can lose, because it's the only thing anyone has.
screen: `THROW THE REST AWAY.` · `EACH LIVES ONLY THIS MOMENT.` · `SHORT LIFE, SMALL CORNER, SHORT FAME.` · `THE ONLY PART YOU CAN STEER.` · then, large: `ONLY THIS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Feel this breath: the cool air coming in, the slight warmth going out. That's it. That's the whole of your life right now. When your mind drifts to earlier today, notice it, and say quietly, gone. When it drifts to later, notice it, and say, unknown. Then come back to this breath. And this one. Only this. The bell holds the time.
Only now. Marcus says each person lives only this moment; the past is already lived, and the future is uncertain. Today's word.
Your line: only this. Three times today, when your mind runs ahead or behind, feel one breath and say: only this. Day five hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius return to Meditations 3.10 when worry or regret pulls at them, bringing their attention back to the present moment.

original.note: Greek, 'the present': the moment Marcus says is all each of us lives.

trapdoor: what you thought: live in the moment.
what it means: the past is finished, the future unknown; this moment is the only place your choices happen.
what a scholar hears: Marcus makes the same point in 2.14: the present is the only thing a person can be deprived of, since it is all they have.

notes: 3.10 paraphrased: throw away all else and hold to these few things; each lives only the present, which is an indivisible point; the rest is either lived or uncertain; short the life, small the corner of earth, short the longest posthumous fame, passed on by poor men who die soon and know not themselves, much less one long dead. Confirm.
Marcus 'writing in a camp on the frontier': Book 3 carries a heading placing it at Carnuntum in most manuscripts. Confirm the heading and its reliability.
Trapdoor cites 2.14 (the present is all a man can lose); confirm.
Greek 'to paron': confirm the phrase as used in 3.10.
